note: The Byzantine Empire formally recognized Charlemagne's imperial title in the Treaty of Aachen (812), negotiated with Emperor Michael I Rhangabe. Byzantium had initially rejected the coronation (800) as usurpation — the Empress Irene's regency created a constitutional argument that the Roman imperial throne was vacant, but Byzantium naturally rejected a western imperial rival. The 12-year negotiation ultimately produced recognition in exchange for Frankish relinquishment of Venetian and Dalmatian territorial claims. The recognition established the 'two emperor' system — East and West — that defined European political theory throughout the medieval period.

_quarry.structural_significance: Byzantine recognition of Charlemagne legitimizes the division of the Roman imperial tradition into eastern and western branches; the 'two emperor' framework creates the constitutional basis for the Holy Roman Empire's claim to equal dignity with Byzantium; Venice and Dalmatia's assignment to Byzantine influence shapes the Adriatic geopolitics for centuries
